families.source: UKHSA management and prevention guidance for GAS and iGAS wound infections in detention settings
families.topic: GAS wound prevention, diagnosis, treatment, IPC and outbreak response in prisons and prescribed places of detention
families.page_title: Management and prevention of group A Streptococcus (GAS and iGAS) wound infections in prescribed places of detention
evidence_points: The guidance applies to prisons, young offender institutions and other prescribed places of detention in England.
It supports collaborative prevention, diagnosis and management of GAS wound infections.
Healthcare, justice, commissioning and health-protection teams have defined roles.
Wound assessment should identify infection signs and risk factors.
Clinical specimens and microbiology support diagnosis and outbreak investigation.
Infection prevention includes hand hygiene, wound care, cleaning and safe equipment practice.
Linked cases require escalation and assessment for a wider incident or outbreak.
Movement and transfer information can be relevant to continuity of care and control.
A wound or positive culture alone does not establish invasive disease or a linked outbreak.
Management requires clinical severity, microbiology, epidemiological links, setting and current specialist advice.

families.source: UKHSA principles for safer visiting during care-home infectious illness outbreaks
families.topic: proportionate visiting decisions, resident wellbeing, risk assessment and outbreak controls in care homes
families.page_title: Supporting safer visiting in care homes during infectious illness outbreaks
evidence_points: The guidance supports proportionate visiting decisions during infectious illness outbreaks in care homes.
Maintaining contact with relatives and friends is important to resident wellbeing.
Outbreak controls should respect private and family life while managing infection risk.
Decisions should consider the pathogen, mode of transmission and severity.
Resident vulnerability and the physical care-home environment affect risk.
Visits into and out of the home may require different controls.
Hand hygiene, ventilation, PPE or other measures may reduce risk where appropriate.
Blanket restrictions should not be applied without a setting-specific risk assessment.
An outbreak declaration does not automatically require stopping all visiting.
Visiting plans require current health-protection advice, resident preferences, legal duties and infection-control evidence.

families.source: UKHSA guidance for acute respiratory infection outbreaks in higher-risk communal accommodation
families.topic: ARI prevention, outbreak assessment, testing, IPC and support in asylum, homeless and refuge accommodation
families.page_title: Acute respiratory infections: outbreaks in higher-risk communal accommodation settings
evidence_points: The guidance applies to higher-risk communal accommodation without onsite clinical teams.
Examples include asylum accommodation, homeless hostels and domestic-abuse refuges.
Shared rooms, bathrooms and facilities can increase transmission opportunities.
Preparedness should include escalation routes, infection-control supplies and communication.
Outbreak assessment considers symptoms, onset dates and possible epidemiological links.
Testing may help identify influenza, COVID-19 or other respiratory pathogens.
Control measures can include ventilation, hygiene, isolation support and reducing mixing.
Residents may need practical support to follow health advice safely.
Multiple respiratory illnesses in a setting do not automatically prove a single linked outbreak.
Response requires linkage, timing, setting vulnerability, testing and local health-protection assessment.

families.source: UKHSA clade I mpox healthcare management update
families.topic: HCID derogation, clinical assessment, IPC, PPE and management of possible clade I mpox
evidence_points: UK chief medical officers agreed that clade I mpox no longer met HCID criteria in March 2025.
Clade I mpox nevertheless remains a potentially serious infection requiring appropriate management.
NHS organisations should update pathways that previously relied on automatic HCID referral.
Clinical assessment should consider symptoms, travel and exposure history.
Possible cases still require prompt MPXV testing and public-health notification.
Healthcare providers should use risk assessment to select appropriate infection-control measures.
PPE requirements depend on the clinical activity and transmission risk.
Admission and transfer decisions should reflect the patient's condition and local capability.
Removal of HCID classification does not mean that suspected cases require no precautions.
Management requires current clinical severity, clade testing, exposure, setting and UKHSA guidance.
